answer_text:
# 🟣 The History of Purple

*From Sea Snails to Synthetic Dye — The Most Regal Colour on Earth*

---

## I. The Ancient World: A Colour Born from the Sea

Purple has one of the most dramatic and unlikely origins of any colour. Known in antiquity as Tyrian purple — also called royal or imperial purple — it is a reddish-purple natural dye secreted by several species of predatory sea snails in the family Muricidae, including *Bolinus brandaris*, *Hexaplex trunculus*, and *Stramonita haemastoma*.

This extraordinary dye was first produced by the Phoenician city of Tyre in the Bronze Age. The very name "Phoenician" may even have meant "purple people," derived from an ancient Greek word for the colour of the mythical phoenix. According to myth, the discovery of purple was credited to the pet dog of Tyros, the mistress of Tyre's patron god Melqart.

The production process was as extraordinary as it was gruelling. In ancient times, extracting this dye involved tens of thousands of snails and substantial labour, and as a result, the dye was highly valued. Dyeing with Murex and Purpura was a complex process which involved extracting the liquid while the mollusc was still alive and exposing it to sunlight for a specified period of time, during which the dye changed colour. It could take up to 12,000 molluscs to produce just 1 gram of dye.

The stench of production was legendary. According to historians of the time, the smell was so diabolical that "purple vats had to be outside the city walls because no one could live next to the horrible smell." Even the clothes that had been dyed with them had a distinctive odour.

Yet what emerged from this foul process was breathtaking. Not only was the dye bright purple — a colour unmatched in the ancient world — but it stayed fast and bright, even after fabrics made with it were washed. It is believed that the intensity of the purple hue actually improved rather than faded as the dyed cloth aged.

---

## II. Antiquity: The Colour of Gods and Emperors

This vibrant colour symbolised power, wealth, and divine authority, spreading across civilisations and influencing art, rituals, and social hierarchies.

Tyrian purple was so highly prized that only kings could afford it, and under the Romans, it was more valuable than gold. The Phoenicians gained great fame as sellers of purple and exported its manufacture to their colonies, notably Carthage, from where it spread in popularity and was adopted by the Romans as a symbol of imperial authority and status.

In Rome, purple became law. The Caesars declared it their official colour and claimed exclusive rights to its production. The most senior Roman magistrates wore a *toga praetexta* — a white toga edged in Tyrian purple. The even more sumptuous *toga picta*, solid Tyrian purple with gold thread edging, was worn by generals celebrating a Roman triumph.

Cleopatra was apparently a huge fan of Tyrian purple; not only did she dress in it, but she also used it for her royal barge, the walls of her palace and even her sofas. Its influence on figures such as Cleopatra, Nero, and Julius Caesar cannot be understated. It was so significant that tradition eventually dictated that purple was only worn by royalty.

---

## III. The Byzantine Empire: Born in the Purple

The Byzantine Empire jealously guarded the colour's exclusivity. The Byzantine Empire continued this legacy, tightly controlling the production of Tyrian purple and subsidising its use exclusively for the colouring of imperial silks. The symbolic term *"porphyrogenitos,"* meaning "born in the purple," emerged in the 9th century to designate a child born to a reigning emperor, further intertwining the colour with imperial lineage.

---

## IV. The Medieval Period: Purple and the Sacred

As the ancient dyeing traditions faded across Europe, purple retained its spiritual and noble associations. Biological pigments were often difficult to acquire, and the details of their production were kept secret by the manufacturers. In antiquity, the Middle Ages and the early modern period, colour often functioned as a status symbol. This is particularly evident in the case of ultramarine, originally derived from the natural stone lapis lazuli. At that time, colour was not merely a design element but an expression of power, importance and value.

Purple remained a symbol of the Church and of royalty throughout medieval Europe, worn by bishops and kings alike — a living memory of imperial Rome.

---

## V. The Accident That Changed Everything: Perkin's Mauve (1856)

For millennia, purple had been the prisoner of wealth, available only to those who could afford thousands of sea snails. Then, in a modest home laboratory in East London, an 18-year-old student changed history forever — entirely by accident.

Mauveine was discovered serendipitously by William Henry Perkin in 1856 while he was attempting to synthesise the phytochemical quinine for the treatment of malaria. Perkin made several attempts at the synthesis over the Easter vacation in his home laboratory, using coal tar as a source of aniline. Oxidising the aniline with potassium dichromate gave a black sludge — which didn't contain aniline. It contained something far more exciting. Perkin noticed whilst cleaning out a flask with ethanol that a purple solution had formed.

The colour became known as mauve, from the French word for the mallow flower, though in 1863 Perkin gave his dye a more scientific name: mauveine.

This discovery brought purple — a colour so expensive it had previously only been afforded by royalty and the Church — to the mass market. Queen Victoria wore a mauve gown to the Royal Exhibition in 1862, and French Empress Eugénie made the shade fashionable at court. Newspapers joked that Britain had caught a case of "mauve measles."

The ripple effects were vast. Perkin paved the way for modern chemistry to move into industrial applications, and indirectly led to advances in modern medicine, explosives, photography, and plastics.

---

## VI. Purple Today: Democracy of a Royal Colour

Purple has travelled an extraordinary arc — from the reeking vats of ancient Phoenicia to the fashion houses of Paris; from the cloaks of Roman emperors to the wardrobes of ordinary Victorians. Purple is still associated with royalty in the West because purple dye was once extremely expensive to manufacture. Yet today, anyone can wear it.

Colour is a journey — from the primal earth pigments of our ancestors to the refined dyes of great traditions. It is both physical and emotional, scientific and artistic. And of all colours, purple perhaps best embodies that journey
